data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A panel of non-experts using a checklist is more reliable than a single expert because the checklist transforms the task from a high-variance 'pattern recognition' problem into a low-variance 'verification' problem, effectively raising the reliability floor.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The task requires synthesis of contradictory evidence that is not captured by the checklist items.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The checklist is insufficiently granular to cover the critical failure modes of the task.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The cost of a single 'miss' by the panel exceeds the benefit of the average reliability gain.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The checklist acts as a low-pass filter that eliminates the 'catastrophic slips' (type I/II errors) common in intuitive expert judgment. While the expert has a higher 'ceiling' of performance, their variance is higher due to cognitive biases (e.g., availability heuristic). The panel's reliability gain is a function of variance reduction rather than increased peak accuracy.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
